Some words belong together. When they do, you never put any punctuation between them. No comma, no colon, no semicolon, and no dash.
Picture those words holding hands. Punctuation is a wall. You never build a wall between two people holding hands.
Here's the method. If the choices only differ by a comma, a colon, or nothing, ask: do the words on each side belong together? If yes, pick no punctuation.
The biggest pair is the who and its did. The scientists who studied the reef published their results. Who: the scientists. Did: published. No comma between them.
Trap alert. The reef, comma, published. That comma splits the who from the did, even though the who is long.
The did and its what also hold hands. The two nations signed the treaty. A colon after signed is wrong, because a colon needs a full sentence before it.
A title right before a name stays together too. Entomologist Heather Grab found something. No commas around the name.
And words like said, found, or showed stay attached to that. The study found that sleep improves reaction time. No comma before that.
Let's try an SAT style question. The scientists who studied the reef, blank, published their results. Choices: comma, colon, semicolon, or no punctuation.
The scientists who studied the reef is the who. Published is the did. They hold hands. The answer is no punctuation.
Trap alert. A long who tempts you to add a comma for a breath. Don't. Length doesn't matter. Who plus did never gets a wall.

Remember three things. Words that belong together hold hands. Never split a who from its did. And when in doubt, ask: do these words belong together? Great work.
